I am 51 years old, and I have farmed these six *mu* of land in Quzhou since I was a young girl. I never went to school — I learned everything from my mother and from watching the neighbors. My husband works in the city now, so the cropping decisions are mine alone. I do not like to gamble with new crops. The wheat–maize rotation has fed my family for generations, and the grain station buys both without fuss. That is what I will plant this year.

The winter wheat went into the ground last October, as it always does. I bought *Luyuan 502* seed from the shop in town because Old Wang next door said it stood up well to the dry winds last spring. The wheat is sleeping now, but I will give it the winter irrigation soon, then the jointing water in March, the heading water in April, and one more before the grain fills in May. Four irrigations total. I cannot afford more — the electricity for the well pump is expensive. For fertilizer, I will spread the compound bag at basal and top-dress with urea twice. The shopkeeper told me the new formula, and I trust him. I rotary-till the wheat field every autumn to break up the corn stubble.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will plant *Denghai 605* corn directly into the stubble without ploughing. At my age, I do not have the strength to till twice in one summer. No-tillage saves me labor and diesel money. The hybrid corn grows fast and thick. I will irrigate it twice — once at the jointing stage and once when the tassels show. I will spray for armyworms and weeds three times if the weather stays humid, fewer if it is dry. I expect the wheat to give me about 500 kg per *mu* and the corn about 550 kg per *mu*. Some I keep for the chickens and our own flour; the rest I sell.
